title: Regression Hunt Chronicle: triage, micro-bisect recipe, and canary comparison notes
content:
Objective:
This is a living chronicle of how we investigate small-to-medium performance regressions across the serving runtime. It focuses on triage sequencing (quick signal checks), a lightweight micro-bisect recipe we use when rollout/canary comparisons are noisy, and pragmatic profiling snippets to get meaningful flamegraphs or CPU/KV-cache attributions quickly.

Audience and scope:
- For on-call SREs, serving-runtime engineers, and applied-ML performance owners.
- Not a full incident writeup template; use this during the first 4–24 hours of a performance regression to determine rollback/fallback or escalate to a deeper investigation.

Quick signal checklist (first 15 minutes) — order matters:
1) Confirm alert validity: which metric fired (p50/p95/p99 latency, reject rate, queue depth, GPU mem pressure, token throughput)? Grab the exact alert window.
2) Count scope: are affected requests localized to a route/model/region/instance-type? Run: 
   - query: SELECT count(*) FROM requests WHERE time BETWEEN t0 AND t1 GROUP BY route, model_variant, region
3) Canary vs baseline: pull canary tag and baseline tag metrics for the same window (5/15/60m). If canary used a config change (batching, kv_cache, quantize), flag that as highest-probability cause.
4) Error vs latency: are we seeing increased errors that imply fallback/retries? If yes, reduce noise by isolating only success responses for latency comparison.
5) External dependencies: check downstream datastore, S3 latency, tokenization microservice. If downstream latency increased, mark low-probability for runtime kernel changes.

Dashboards and panels to open immediately:
- Per-route latency heatmap (5s resolution) with percentiles and sample rate.
- Token-level time-per-op panel (tokenization / forward-pass / kv-restore / postproc).
- GPU utilization and GPU PCIe stall counters (if available).
- Autoscaler and queue-length panels.
- Canary vs baseline overlay chart for chosen route/model.
Note: If the alert window is >15 minutes ago, expand sliding windows (5m -> 1h -> 6h) to find onset.

A lightweight micro-bisect recipe (10–90 minutes) — for noisy regressions where a full git bisect is expensive:
1) Define two stable snapshots: last-known-good (LKG) commit/config and first-known-bad (FKB) commit/config. Collect the serving config blob for both.
2) Build an A/B canary in a single region: split traffic 10/90 to LKG and FKB using traffic routing. Keep sampling at request-id level.
3) Instrumented sampling: capture N=500 full traces from both cohorts, flagged in trace metadata with cohort=LKG|FKB. Ensure sampling preserves request hash distribution (use same route + same client-id segments).
4) Run simple comparative aggregations: median latency, p95, 99, and tail-n with tail-n defined by token count buckets. Also compute CPU time per token and KV-lookup count per request.
5) If results are ambiguous: escalate to targeted microbench (see next section). Otherwise, proceed with rollback or fix candidate.

Targeted microbench steps (30–120 minutes) — reproduce locally in perf-lab or short-lived cluster:
- Generate representative workloads: use production sampled prompts (strip PII) and preserve token length distribution.
- Run the forward-pass profiler with these knobs:
  * trace-level sampling: collect per-layer time and memory (top 10 sequences)
  * GPU counters: kernel duration histogram, gemm occupancy, and memory copy time
  * KV cache timings: store/retrieve latency, per-request hit/miss ratio
- Useful profiling commands (examples):
  - capture traces: curl -H "X-Profile: full" https://internal-inference/route?sample=1 > trace.json
  - flamegraph generator: ./tools/convert_prof_to_flame trace.json > trace.folded; ./tools/flamegraph.pl trace.folded > flame.svg
  - cpu sample: perf record -F 200 -g -- ./serve_binary --replay workload.trace; perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded

Attribution heuristics (how we decide cause):
- If compute kernel times (GEMM/attn) are up across the stack: suspect model change, kernel selection, or tensor layout differences from quantization.
- If tokenization or postproc spikes: suspect prompt-parsing changes, new sys-prompt insertion, or routing-layer middleware regressions.
- If KV-cache hit-rate drops and tail latency increases: likely caching-key format or invalidation bug. Cross-check cache version in the rollout metadata.
- If CPU scheduling or GC jumps on CPU-only hosts: look for dependency upgrades that changed memory behavior (e.g., allocator or Python runtime).

Canary comparison checklist (what to capture for each canary experiment):
- full snapshot of the serving config (models, quantization profile, batcher configs, kernel hints)
- exact commit hashes for runtime, model-compiler, and any relevant libs (cuDNN/CUDA container tag)
- traffic shaping rules used (weights, sticky hashing)
- sample of request payloads and token-length histogram
- artifact-size and model weight fingerprints (for quantized variants)

Edge cases we frequently hit:
- "Noisy baseline": when baseline has transient spikes, the comparison window needs smoothing and repeat experiments at a different time-of-day. Document baseline noise and rerun.
- "Heterogeneous hardware masking": regressions that appear only on certain GPU generations because kernel fallback code path changed — remember to compare per-instance-type.
- "Autoscaler thrash": sometimes latency increases are due to scaling windows and cold-starts rather than model runtime; correlate with node join/leave events.

Decision matrix (quick):
- Confirmed code/config change + regression replicated in canary -> block rollout / revert.
- No change in canary but production still noisy -> widen sampling, check external dependencies, re-evaluate alert thresholds.
- Regression only in a subset of instance types -> limit rollout to unaffected instance types and open eng bug.

Post-triage notes (what to include in a short handoff message):
- Short summary (2–3 lines) with affected routes/models and impact estimate (p50/p99 increase and QPS affected).
- Canary status and whether we reverted or changed traffic rules.
- Primary suspect with brief evidence (e.g., "attn kernel time +45% on xG-100, KV hit-rate dropped from 0.83 -> 0.62").
- Next owner and ETA for full root cause.

Quick checklist for postmortem capture (when the incident becomes an RCA):
- store all sampled traces and profiling artifacts in the incident archive (S3 path) with tags cohort/LKG/FKB, route, and timestamp.
- collect perf recordings and flamegraphs for top 3 offending stacks.
- layout the commit/config diff and candidate root changes.
- include small reproduction script that runs in perf-lab.

Open questions / TODOs (work items to improve our first-response efficacy):
- Automate cohort-sampling for any active rollout so we can instantly compare LKG vs current with a single dashboard toggle.
- Add a tiny playback harness that can push a 1k sample workload to perf-lab with identical hash distribution as production.
- Surface per-kernel GPU metrics in main latency dashboard (currently buried under hardware).

Notes to self / shorthand observations seen in recent runs:
- When quantization profile changed from int8v1 -> int8v2, we saw a 7% p95 cost but a 15% CPU-side prep-time increase; this pointed at slower layout transpositions before GEMM.
- KV-cache invalidation was introduced by a config toggle that serialized keys differently; it only surfaced on multi-tenant shared caches.

Contact/backups:
- Primary: Evelyn Park (owner on-call)
- Backup: Samir Gupta
- Escalation: Lina Chen (perf lead)

If you use parts of this chronicle in an RCA, please add the link to linked_artifacts and mark status->final.
